utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, The Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Could the witness be escorted in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I don't know if Your Honours have any preliminaries. We have one that we could handle while the witness is coming in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we had yesterday filed a waiver for attendance for General Mladic tomorrow. We are now putting on the record that we are withdrawing that waiver. The plans have changed in terms of the visits that were envisioned at the UNDU. And the general will need to be transported here and will be with us tomorrow during the proceedings. I wanted to put that on the record in time for all of the arrangements that need to be made can be made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear. We wonder, the next witness who was on the list will not appear. Will the witness after that be moved forward?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, we're just assuming based upon the estimates that this witness may continue for part of the day tomorrow. It may not be. It may be out of an overabundance of caution I just want to make sure that is on the record at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see that. But it means that we couldn't fill the whole of the day tomorrow if the Prosecution concludes its cross-examination relatively early.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours, we could not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Professor Stankovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration that you've given at the beginning of your testimony, and we'll now continue. Mr. Ivetic will resume his examination-in-chief. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. And we have provided, I believe, to Your Honours, hard copies with the English of P7444, which is the Clark autopsy summary list. P7445, which is the -- just a summation list. Also a hard copy of Dr. Stankovic's report in English. And in English -- pardon me. In English, the Bosnian autopsy records. The Prosecution has also received a copy, and I believe that -- that Dr. Stankovic already has his B/C/S copies of the Bosnian autopsy specialists at happened as well as a B/C/S copy of the P7444, since those are the ones he was referring -- referring us to yesterday, but if I'm mistaken I ask that the Professor let us know. I can then provide copies of each as we go through them if need be.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a copy of the autopsy reports in Serbian. I mean, those drawn up by the Bosnian pathologists, as well as the ones drawn up by Dr. Clark.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Then, professor, I would wish you a good morning.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I would ask that we call up, again, the report of Dr. Stankovic, which is D1447, MFI, and if we could turn to page 11 in the English, and that will be page 16, I believe, in the Serbian. We had left off, just about to move onto case number 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will be tendering all of the Bosnian autopsy reports I mentioned, so to save time, I will tender the ones that we've already covered and the ones we are yet to cover at the end dealing with all of Tomasica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, mainly the Bosnian autopsy reports were missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Most of part of the rest was available, but it's good to have it all together. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And looking now -- I apologise. Does everyone have e-court available? I seem not to. Okay. Looking at case number 3, professor, there appears to be a discussion on the one hand of a blunt force trauma. Can you first begin by telling us how a blunt force trauma compares to a gun-shot injury.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Blunt force trauma is an injury with specific characteristics manifested on the bodies of victims, if we are talking about bones, with depressed fractures of bones in the direction of the force. Sometimes they may retain the shape of the blunt instrument with which the instrument [as interpreted] was caused. On the soft tissues, they are noted as lacerations with hematoma or skin abrasions. As for gun-shot injuries, their look is completely different, depending on the angle at which a bullet entered the body. The entry wound may be round or oval in shape. If it was caused from a certain distance, it may have a depression ring and some other characteristics. I think I don't need to list them all now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in relation to case number 3, the Bosnian autopsy is 65 ter number 33731 for those who have the binders, and ... yeah. And, professor, could you briefly just tell us why you chose to highlight this case as to both Dr. Clark and the Bosnian pathologist, Dr. Durmisevic. What was the main thing that struck you from comparing the two?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this specific case, Dr. Durmisevic describes in the autopsy report on page 2 under item 4, an injury with two depressions of the cranial vault behind the coronal suture on the parietal bones with a stair phenomenon to be noted on the right. Fractures spread out from the depressed area, whereas in Dr. Clark's autopsy report, it does not mention this injury at all. It is neither described nor is it stated what was the instrument that caused it. And another thing: Dr. Clark, on page 21 in the Serbian version, says that the injuries were probably -- they probably occurred post-mortem, most of the right ribs, the angles of the third and the seventh rib, the injuries to most of the ribs on the axilla line and the angles of the fourth and fifth ribs probably occurred after death. The fractures occurred after death. The right radius and ulna, that is to say the bones of the right lower arm, and the post-mortem injury to the upper part of the right fibula. In the autopsy report of Dr. Durmisevic, there is no description of the said injuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And then if we could move to case number 4, which is on our screen in both languages. And the Bosnian autopsy is 65 ter number 33732. And if I can ask you to highlight for the Trial Chamber why you chose to -- to compare this -- this case between Dr. Clark's findings and that of Dr. Durmisevic.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the autopsy report on page 2, Dr. Durmisevic, under item 2, injuries, notes, inter alia, fractures of cervical vertebra from the second to the sixth whereas Dr. Clark in his finding does not mention the existence of such injuries of the cervical vertebra. In his finding, Dr. Clark notes that there are post-mortem fractures, that is to say, fractures occurring after death, of several left ribs. The right diaphysis of the right humerus, that is to say, the right upper arm and the medial diaphysis of the left ulna. And Dr. Durmisevic failed to describe such injuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And given the nature of the discrepancies we have gone through thus far and that have you seen, could a professional like Dr. John Clark noticed the discrepancies, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If he had insight --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. MacDonald.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Just with regard to my friend' question if Mr. John Clark noticed the discrepancies, I believe -- I don't have the transcript page at hand, but I believe Dr. Clark stated he hadn't seen the autopsy reports of the Bosnian pathologists. No foundation for this question, if this was the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we do not know. We do not know what time-frame Mr. Ivetic has on his mind and whether he has -- but however valid it may be, I do not know. Then it would certainly be something for cross-examination. Mr. Ivetic, at the same time, you've heard --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yeah --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the comment. So, therefore, if Mr. MacDonald would be right, you might find his reason to reconsider your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will. Let me ask a different question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Professor, if you had two pathologists working together and generating reports on the same body, what is the normal procedure? Do they communicate with one another; and, if so, how?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the work of two pathologists who are processing mortal remains of a single body, they communicate with each other. They consult each other about the registered injuries and the instruments by which the injuries were inflicted. In this specific case, I believe that both the -- both pathologists, Dr. Durmisevic and Dr. Clark, if they saw the other autopsy report, would certainly notice the discrepancies, and after that, they would probably try to harmonise their views.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to -- to save time, I'd like to look at case number 8 which is on page 13 in the English, and it should be, I think, page 17 in the Serbian. It's going to be the next page in the Serbian; I apologise. I keep forgetting to add a page to the hard copy. I guess it's actually going to be one more page. 18. Okay. Here, in number 8, and that's 65 ter number 33736 in the Bosnian autopsy reports, and here we have one of the pathologists indicating a "hard and blunt, probably," and then something with a question mark, "bevelled implement, though blows inflicted with a sharp tool cannot be excluded," and then we have the other pathologist saying gun-shot injury to the neck. In your opinion, can two pathologists come up with these descriptions for the same body, for the same injuries in the same body?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is a fact that in his opinion, Professor Sarajlic noted in paragraphs 2 and 3 that the injuries to the neck area may have been caused by a hard and blunt probably bevelled implement though blows inflicted with a sharp tool cannot be excluded either. By contrast, Dr. Clark says that a probable gun-shot injury has been inflicted to the neck. Such conclusions necessitate the harmonisation of views between two pathologists because if the vertebra are hit with a hard and blunt instrument then the manner of fracture is different than the fractures caused by the impact of a bullet, and especially if this is blunt force trauma and a bevelled implement such as an axe, then the look of the fracture of the vertebra would be different than if they had been caused by a bullet, or a gun-shot injury.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'd like to look at item number C of your report which starts on page 13 in the English but case number 1 is on the next page, page 14 in the English and it will be page 20 in the Serbian of your report, and the Bosnian autopsy is 65 ter number 33738, and in Clark, this will be at page 25 of P07444. And you have one case listed here. Can you tell us in relation to the finding of the Bosnian pathologist and as to Dr. Clark what is it about these finds that caused you to select this case, to highlight in part C as unacceptable conclusions?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Durmisevic, on page 2 under item, injuries, describes a multi-fragmented fracture of the basis of the skull and bones of the face with missing fragments, and fractures spreading out towards the crown of the skull. That's more or less the description of the injury noted. And then, under item 2, opinion, nature of injury to the skull, even though there is no clearly visible entry wound, it corresponds to the impact of a bullet, a high-caliber and high-velocity bullet, which causes significant fragmentation of the bone as well as fissures spreading out across the crown of the skull. The most probable direction of the bullet is from the occipital area towards the bones of the face which are fragmented. This is Dr. Durmisevic's description. Dr. Clark, on page 37 of the Serbian version, says the following: "Gun-shot injury to the head with the entry hole probably to the back of the head in the left lower occipital area where significant damage spreading downwards may be noted. It seems that the exit wound is on the front side where the lower part of the forehead bone and the face are fragmented and mandibula is present in the middle part and at the left angulus." It is not possible to conclude from this description whether the entry wound on the head bones is in the occipital area as described by Dr. Durmisevic and Dr. Clark as well. There is no description that would note the caving in of bones, a caved-in fragment of bone that was found with surface damage in the form of bones bevelled towards the inside, and here I have in mind the occipital bones, those on the back of the head. So no such descriptions are provided but a specific conclusion is drawn, and when you just read the text without having other documents at your disposal, you cannot conclude that this was, indeed, the trajectory of the bullet. I note once again the description of the injury provided by Dr. Durmisevic, which I now read out.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, could we always try because I'm a bit lost this, that, that there, compare this T number, so and so, so that I can follow it. I'm still with the previous one, if you would allow me to ask one question. For the previous one you described, where you said that the findings of what possibly or probably would have been established, both experts conclude that the cause of death was unascertained and therefore is unknown so -- and they do that one on the basis of probabilities, the other one on the basis of possibilities. But finally they say: We don't know. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So in their conclusion, there is no disagreement at all. There are in some details of the description of the injuries, they seem to differ of opinion on -- on -- on -- on what it exactly is, and they both explain that it's very difficult to assess what is there and they're talking in terms of probabilities rather than in establishing anything for certain. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Talking about the cause of death, neither of them stated it. And that's all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... for the previous one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the previous one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the previous case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... they say it is unascertained. They can't establish it. To that extent, they do express themselves, and if you say, They don't give a statement about that, the statement is that they don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not say that they did not say anything. I said the same thing as you, that the cause of death has not been ascertained, so that's what it is. But what they do not agree about is that the description of the injury to the bones of the skull which are fractured. One of them says it's in the area of the back of the neck. One of them says that the injuries --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... we have heard all that. But you earlier expressed yourself on what a court needs. If a court receives a clear conclusion by two experts that the cause of death could not be established, then that has consequences, perhaps, for the court. A court might say under those circumstances, we can't consider this as a murder or whatever, because we don't know how that person died. At least not on the basis of the autopsies. What -- why -- and that's what you emphasise again and again, why would we know for certain that the expert was -- were also in agreement on what they saw on the jaw or on the left lower leg if the conclusions are that, at least on this basis, we couldn't -- we couldn't establish how this person died? Why do we need all that? Because you expressed yourself on it. I'm interested to know what you think we would need.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because each injury has its characteristics. One pathologist cannot describe an injury caused by a blunt force trauma as if were a gun-shot injury. What would that be about? It would turn out that one of the experts cannot distinguish between gun-shot injuries and blunt force trauma or that one and the same type of injury is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... they are talking in terms of probabilities and possibilities, which explains already why, perhaps, they do not agree. But my question was not the issue you are raising in your answer. My question was: Why do you think that we would need all kind of details if, I would say, in favour of the Defence, that's at least what it looks like, the experts agree they couldn't establish the cause of death and, therefore, it may become irrelevant in the context of this case. Why would we need to know exactly why the one says it is probable, why the other says it's possible? Why would we need to know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not... in fact, I am called by the Defence as an expert in this case. But I'm primarily presenting my expert opinion and views on the documents which are in the case file based on my knowledge. The generally accepted view in forensic medicine is that all injuries present on the body during autopsy should be verified. If one injury is not verified by a pathologist, that speaks of his attitude to his job. There cannot be injuries, for instance, to the cervical part of the spine inflicted in one way --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you have explained that now several times. You have not answered my question yet. I leave it to the parties whether you want to follow up on what I raised. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think he has answered the question where he says it speaks to the attitude of the pathologist to his job so it goes to the credibility of a witness that was brought here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question was why we would have to know it. That was the question. He has not answered that question, I think. Unless he thinks that we should know the attitude, if we are talking about results of -- of expert expertise and the witness apparently ignored that where they say probably, possibly, et cetera that has already -- it has got nothing to do with attitude but a good expression of uncertainty, if you are not certain about what you see.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So is it the position of this Trial Chamber that if the methodology of a Prosecution expert was bad, but he happened to get the right result that is not a matter that should be brought before the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not saying that, Mr. Ivetic, and you know that. But let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm hearing that from you. That's how I'm interpreting these words, that's why I'm asking for instruction and guidance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, then you misinterpreted my words. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Without guidance, I cannot proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are invited to proceed and if you can't, then do what you think you should do if you would not proceed. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In relation to case number 1, under item C, professor, is there anything else from the standpoint of forensic medicine that is significant to you that you think we need to know to appraise the methodology and credibility of the work of either the Bosnian pathologists or Dr. Clark?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Case C?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... it's under C, it's case number 1 which is on page number 20 in the Serbian. It's on our screen now. The case of ...

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which -- because I think I gave some kind of instructions in this respect. That's what 65 ter number, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: 65 ter number 33738, as I had already indicated previously, and that is P7444, page 25, as I also had previously indicated. And it's page 14 in the English of the document that we have on our screen right now which is D1447, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. MacDonald.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I would object to this question on the basis that, from Professor Stankovic's report, the only disputed finding he has written down is the one that's been discussed about the direction of the trajectory of the bullet. And I think my friend is now seeking to bring out other differences which Professor Stankovic hasn't noted in his report, and therefore hasn't noticed to the Prosecution that should have been done in an expert report. That would be the objection to this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, this objection is denied, although, of course, it's preferable that the relevant information is contained in the report. It does not exclude for asking for anything in addition to what is written in the report already. So, therefore, could the witness answer the question. Which was: What in case 1 is there -- whether there's anything else, from the standpoint of forensic medicine, that is significant to you and you think we need to know to appraise the methodology and credibility of the work of either the Bosnian pathologists or Dr. Clark. Could you answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think there are no more important elements apart from the ones I've already said.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Then if we could move to the next page in the Serbian - stay on the same page in the English - we have your opinions listed on that page, and I would ask, do you stand behind everything written in this part?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by what I've written and what has been submitted to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The Defence would tender D1447 MFI, and we would also tender the Bosnian autopsies which are 65 ter number 33730 through 65 ter number 33737 for cases 2 through 9 in part B in order, and 65 ter number 33738, which relates to case 1 under item C.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I interrupt just before we tender. I just have a question on D1447, MFI. Doctor, at page 14 in English under heading D, Opinion about analysis in question, you state that: "... it is the obligation of all experts who took part or are still taking part in investigation procedures, establishing truth and determining the sentence, to work on the basis of facts in a generally accepted professional manner and within the framework of the existing legal norms and thus establish the actual truth, name of the [sic] offender and render judgement based on the established facts." My question to you is how is it in the remit of pathologists to determine sentence and to name the offender and render judgement; and if so, could we get authority for this, and how they do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I first said that pathologists determine the truth. Pathologists participate in the work of the judicial authorities by way of producing their reports. I said so at the beginning of the sentence. However, it is the obligation of all the people participating in investigation activities. It's not just the pathologists that participated in the investigation. The whole activity is led by prosecutors. They participate in the investigation, along with ballistics experts, archaeologists, anthropologists. They all participate in the presentation of evidence, and the court is in charge of pinning down liability. If all this had been harmonized in the pre-investigation procedure, as I've said a number of times, I wouldn't be here, and I would not be making objections to the work of Dr. Clark or Dr. Durmisevic or professor Sarajlic. I am not taking part in rendering the judgement. I'm just explaining, from my point of view, as an expert witness, certain findings made by my colleagues, and it is up to you whether you will accept them or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My question is actually part of the process of attempting to accept your comments. You probably were misinterpreted, I don't know. How far, in the English translation of your opinion about the analysis in question, and I thought analysis in question is the analysis of these three experts who are pathologists, you talk of determining the -- establishing the actual truth. I don't know what you may have written in the B/C/S. So when you say you didn't refer to the truth I'm rather surprised. Secondly, I just wanted to say to you, my understanding of this opinion that you are rendering, I didn't accept -- understand it to be of all experts, including anthropologists. I thought you were opining on the work of these three pathologists, and in any case, whoever you may be referring to, my question with respect to the name of the offender, rendering judgement, still stand. You haven't answered that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was talking about the truth that I was analysing from my point of view. That's the work of the pathologist. In the conclusion it says over there the exhumations of the mortal remains from the mass grave of Tomasica contains considerable unclarified areas and questions that remain without answer. The questions put here do not aim to dispute the data collected concerning the death of the people whose bodies were found in the Tomasica mass grave. However, it is the obligation of all the people who participated in the investigation, or are participating in the investigation, determining the truth and establishing a sentence is to determine the real truth within the limits of legal norms and make a judgement. So it is up to us, based on these objections, if there was a discrepancy, to ask the question: Why weren't their views harmonised? That is the main objection. I also believe that Dr. Durmisevic and Dr. Clark and Dr. Sarajlic would find it very easy to narrow their differences and come to the same conclusion. Do they have the same view about the same issue, the same autopsy? Is it necessary to have the same autopsy report, i.e. the same description of injuries? I think the answer is yes. Whether an expert will interpret those injuries in one way or another, that's up to the expert, but he will make a finding by communicating with another expert who performed the same autopsy. For you, as the Trial Chamber, I think that this truth is something that will be decisive in determining the sentence, but we are not interfering in that part of your job. Neither am I interfering. I just want a unified view by experts to be presented to the Trial Chamber, and the Trial Chamber will then make its own decision about what to accept or not. It never happened that a forensic medical expert asked to decide himself how long a sentence should be or to determine whether someone is guilty or not. This conclusion should just serve to come to the truth, the medical truth that has to do with medical reports. I do not go beyond that. And the way that autopsy findings are presented to the Trial Chamber will form the basis, practically, of how the Trial Chamber will decide, whether to acquit or to convict somebody. Nothing more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Obviously we're talking at cross purposes. I don't think there's any point in me pursuing the matter. Thank you very much. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it Mr. Ivetic is invited to continue his comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My apologies, I just --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Apology accepted and not necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To continue, you were tendering quite a number of documents. I invited the registrar to assign numbers and then Judge Moloto had a question. Mr. Registrar, you have had ample time now to --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. 65 ter numbers 33730 through to 65 ter 33738 will be assigned exhibit numbers D1451 through to D1459 respectively, and perhaps under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, let me see. Was that all you tendered? I don't think we had. But let's first deal with those. These are the Bosnian reports. I think it would be wise to have them under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Therefore, D1451 through to D1459 are admitted into evidence, under seal. Mr. Registrar, the remaining tendered documents. There were others.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The remaining already has a number. It was marked for identification so I was just making sure on the record that it is tendered, but I understand the procedure for experts is that Your Honours will decide at the conclusion of the evidence. So I think Mr. Registrar was correct in -

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's not really tendering at this moment. We will wait to decide on what is already tendered and what is now marked for identification. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Professor, I'd now like to return to the report of Dr. Dunjic as to the Srebrenica grave-sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So, thus if we can have D1448, marked for identification in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I believe -- could you confirm if you have a hard copy of the same in Serbian before you, sir? Professor, do you have a hard copy in Serbian of Dr. Dunjic's report?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And I would ask that we turn to page 11 in English and it will be page 10 in the Serbian of the same. Pardon me, it will be the next ... we have here the comment -- it will be on the next page, actually, in the B/C/S. We have here the comment of Dr. Dunjic. It is at the bottom of the first paragraph in both languages. And it reads: "Most of the pathologists engaged to perform autopsies provided in the report final diagnoses without a description of the injuries, instead of providing an objective finding and description of the changes observed, and the conclusions of gun-shot injuries or injuries caused by fire-arms are therefore, effectively, merely diagnoses that are now not verifiable." Professor, first, could you explain for us what is the final diagnoses in the autopsy process so we have that clear?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, it's necessary to describe the changes, describe the injury, and based on the characteristics of a specific injury, you make a conclusion about the nature of the injury. Professor Dunjic noted that some people just wrote down a diagnosis without any description of the injury, and from the view of forensic medicine, it's unacceptable. Nobody is disputing whether it's a blast injury or a gun-shot injury, but it was necessary for people who conducted the autopsies to also describe the injuries in the generally accepted way.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you join in Dr. Dunjic's conclusion as stated here, his -- his criticism?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What is the significance of the lack of detail in the description of injuries; that is to say, what does it do as to the validity of the findings and their ability to be verified?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the validity of the findings, I don't have the right to call it into question, but I cannot verify whether the finding is based on the description of the injury. I have to believe that it's a blast wound or a gun-shot injury from what is written. I just have to take their word for it. I cannot see the characteristics of the injury myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we move to the bottom of page 11 in both languages, we will see Dr. Clark's explanation as to the Kozluk grave for the differing levels of preservation of the bodies in that grave. In your opinion, are there possible and reasonable explanations for varying levels of preservation of bodies in the same grave?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are reasonable explanations. I discussed them yesterday or the day before, and I stand by the opinion I presented. Varying degrees of decomposition in the Kozluk mass grave can be explained in several ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And if it were the case, as Dr. Clark has stated, that this was due to the respective position in the grave, the preservation of the bodies, forensically speaking, what bodies would be expected to be more preserved and what should be recorded in the records of the exhumation as to those bodies? Where would they be situated in the grave?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What Dr. Clark put is one of the possibilities. It's usual for bodies towards the surface of a mass grave closer to the ground to be more decomposed than the bodies that are deeper in the ground and covered by other bodies. In this specific case, we have instances when numbers were distributed, of exhumation in these locations, that some bodies that were buried deeper were more decomposed and more soft tissue was missing than in the bodies closer to the surface.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could focus on that. Where you say there was some bodies that were more decomposed deeper in the grave than at the surface, what does your experience tell you in relation to Dr. Clark's explanation? What do those facts and your experience tell you as to Dr. Clark's explanation as to their preservation level?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that bodies on the surface decompose faster. In the interpretation I had, it was those deeper. No, it's not true. Bodies closer to the surface decompose faster and the tissue is lost faster on them, and the process of skeletonization is, therefore, faster. As for the question about my experience, my experience is similar to the experience described here, but, again, that depends on several factors, and the explanation given by Dr. Clark in this specific instance can be accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what I was trying to do is -- I should have done it in a different way. I was trying to clarify what may be a translation error, but in the last answer you were quoted in saying: "In this specific case, we have instances when numbers were distributed in this location that some bodies that were deeper were more decomposed and more tissue was missing than in the bodies closer to the surface." That's the English that we received from your answer, and I wanted to see with you if that is correct or if you said something different.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, what I said is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And does that raise any concerns or questions about the usual level of preservation of bodies based upon their position in the grave?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, in this case, the position in the grave does not affect the level of decomposition. There are some other factors that could be more important. First of all, how much time the body has been in open air, whether it was affected by animals and insects; third, the time of death could be different to the time of death of the other bodies in the mass grave, but these are just possibilities that I cite in this specific case.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think we're at the time for the break under today's schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we are. Professor Stankovic, we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes. You may follow the usher now. Mr. Ivetic, in terms of time, where are we?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think hour 20, hour 30 and we should be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say one hour. Mr. Registrar, could you tell us where we are?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar tells me that you have got one hour and ten minutes left so it's a little bit over one hour, so let's try to wrap up. But that's not far from one hour and 20. One hour and 15 would even be exactly in the middle of the two. Let's try and see whether we can conclude your examination-in-chief very early in the -- not in the next session but in the session after that. And the assessment, Mr. MacDonald, about cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Three and a half hours, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Three and a half hours. And it remains unchanged based on what you have heard until now?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: It does, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break, and we resume at 25 minutes past 10.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Professor, I'd like to take up where we left off and deal still with these bodies of differing levels of decomposition in Kozluk. Given what you told us about the positioning of these bodies in the grave and the various possible causes for the varying states of decomposition, can one forensically exclude the possibility that these bodies in this mass grave do not date all from the same time-period?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bodies in the Kozluk grave are such that their deaths may have occurred at different periods of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, when we are talking about periods, is that -- are you talking in terms of periods of weeks or months or years or -- I mean, "periods" is a rather undefined -- do you think, for example, that they could be from -- well, three years' difference, one from another or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, considering the decomposition of the soft tissue structures, the death of these persons could have occurred at different times with the difference being several weeks or even several months between them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now if we can move to page 12 in the English, it will be the third paragraph from the top and page 12 in Serbian. And... strike that. We've already covered that one, I apologise. If we could turn to page 13 in the English, it's the third paragraph, and page 13 in the Serbian as well, and that will be the first paragraph. Here it is said that in addition to injuries from high velocity rifles, corpses found at Glogova 2 contained occasional shotgun pellets. Given your knowledge of the military gained through your career, are you able to tell us whether or not shotguns were official weapons within the standard arsenals of the armies on the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The former Yugoslav army did not have any weapons with pellets.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 14 in both languages and it will be the middle of the page in the English, and it will be the first full paragraph at the top in Serbian, and here, it says: "J Clark says probably and W Haglund concludes that the shots were fired at close range but logical as this may seem, there is no evidence of close-range in the autopsy reports, 'the bodies at Ravnice were not buried but lying largely on the surface and thus greatly broken up and scattered. None were blindfolded and none of them had any blast damage but they nearly all still died from gun-shot injuries'." In your opinion, medically speaking, would you except that such evidence of close-range gun-shot wounds would survive after so many years?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I talked about that yesterday or the day before, and I said that some evidence such as burn traces on the bones, the presence of unburned gunpowder traces and presence of metals such as zinc or lead which do not burn may have been proven by microscopic scanning, and the evidence of burning of bones could not have disappeared even if the bodies had been underground for five years.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you go with Dr. Dunjic's observation here as to the -- as to what both Drs. Clark and Mr. Haglund said as to the wounds given that they did not have any observations of such material in their reports?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the observations about the presence of traces of gunpowder explosion on the bodies that were examined?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the description of injuries in autopsy reports, there's no information about the traces of gunpowder explosion. I think that such conclusions of Dr. Haglund is unacceptable considering that we may state our opinion only about what is verified and established rather than on the basis of assumptions. That is what's unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now if we could turn to page 16 in the English, and it will be page 15 in the Serbian, and in this part of Dr. Dunjic's report, there's talk about bodies in Paklenik cave which have been there since 1992 according to other evidence. And the observation that they demonstrate a similar description of putrefaction as some of the remains that are said to be directly linked to Srebrenica. Do you have any additional comments as to what Dr. Dunjic has written here?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's possible depending on the time that the mortal remains were on the surface of the ground, whether they were affected by insects and animals, also the type of soil that they were on, certain aspects of putrefaction may have been similar to that present at other bodies that were found in and around Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Next I want to look at part 2 of Dr. Dunjic's report and this will be on page 17 in English and in Serbian, and the part I want to ask about is item number B, first of all, that reads: "In their autopsy reports, when discussing the cause of death and the occurrence of injuries ante-mortem, all Prosecution experts rely on a method of assuming the cause of death, which leads to an incorrect or unreliable result. In the autopsy reports themselves, no evidence has been provided that the injuries were sustained in life." First of all, do you agree with Dr. Dunjic's criticism of the Prosecution experts in this part?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are no acceptable medical criteria on the basis of which one could determine injuries to the bones in life after the body had been buried and covered by soil for several years, and I agree with that. As for the assumptions of the cause of death, I've said yesterday that judging by the look of the putrefaction and saponification or skeletonization of bodies, one cannot say with certainty what the cause of death was, but in the autopsy report it may be stated that the injuries may have caused death and I think that's a generally accepted position and there's nothing to be said about that. No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, when you refer to the report of Dr. Dunjic, which referred to the cave in June 1992, I think, you left out "probably," but I take it that you wanted to include that in your [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise. If it was left out, it was intended to be there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we look at item A under this part of Dr. Dunjic's report, says, "There are professional standards in forensic practice require a conclusion on the cause of death to be based only an objective finding. An objective finding must be verifiable by any expert, transparent. In order for it to be verifiable there must be a full and detailed description of every injury. This is the standard of forensic practice in Europe." Do you agree with Dr. Dunjic in this respect?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now if we could turn together to page 18 in the English and it will be 18 in the Serbian, the third and the fourth paragraphs from the top, and they read: "It is also important for the Tribunal to note the existence of the so-called post-mortem injuries, these are injuries inflicted on the body after the cessation of the main vital functions. They can have all the characteristics (especially in case of bones) of fractures that occur in living people, but without the ante-mortem attributes." And also the next paragraph that follows after that. Would you offer any additional comments here in relation to these two paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I agree with these two paragraphs as written by Dr. and Professor Dunjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we could turn to page 19 in the English, it will be on the top, and it's the second-to-last paragraph on page 18 in the Serbian and it reads: "In my professional assessment, based on my experience and practice in the forensic autopsy of the exhumed bodies, the classical forensic descriptive method should have been used - a detailed description of all the observed injuries and the condition in which a body was found (which was, unfortunately, done only partially and by a small number of pathologists)." First of all, could you briefly define for us this classical forensic descriptive method.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That implies a very detailed description of all the injuries and changes to the mortal remains during the post-mortem examination. That means locating the injury precisely, describing the look and the shape, the size, the edges and sides of the injured part, whether it's soft tissue or bone, the presence or absence of parts of the injured bone. This is a rule of the so-called Belgrade school to which Professor Dunjic belonged, which was formed by Professor Milovanovic, and in accordance with which I was educated. So, therefore, this is what I accept.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could then move to page 19 in the English and it will be the fifth paragraph from the top, and it will be on the same page in Serbian but it is the third paragraph. And here, we see the comment: "The medico-legal backgrounds from which each of them came are indeed evident from the autopsy records from the Nova Kasaba (1, 2, and 3), Pilica, Sandici, Potocari, Bisina, Glogova Liplje 4, Bisina, Potocari, Lazete, Konjevic Polje, and other sites, I would just point out one thing here, instead of reports (trauma report) the the autopsies were mainly conducted by pathologists rather than experts in forensic medicine, and they provided final diagnosis, conclusions or even final opinions, due to which it is now impossible to check their finding, and therefore also their diagnosis. This raises doubts about the objectivity of the reports." Do you agree with Dr. Dunjic has expressed here about the autopsies?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only say that I agree with the first part as this is the procedure that is applied and that is acceptable. As for the second, that this raises doubts about the objectivity of the report, I would rather not comment on that for a number of reasons. I have no evidence to doubt the findings.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. But do you agree with the part that says it is now impossible to check their findings and therefore also their diagnosis?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that a new post-mortem examination could not find the same state of mortal remains, so now, without the description of the condition, which is provided only as a written diagnosis, rather than as a detailed description of the look and location where the injuries were found, it's very difficult to verify such conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we could turn to page 20 in English, it will be the first paragraph and it's still on page 19 in the Serbian and it's the last paragraph on the page. "Under the subheading, limitations of the pathology evidence on page 2 of the aggregate reports," then there's the ERN number, "... for the sites listed (Kozluk, Nova Kasaba, Konjevic Polje and Glogova) the pathologist J. Clark stated as follows: 'While conscious of these theoretical difficulties, this report is nonetheless compiled on the assumption that the vast majority of the gun-shot and other relevant injuries which were found occurred in life and were, or contributed to, the cause of death. To assume otherwise would be to make any further analysis of the findings virtually meaningless'." What are your professional comments as to what is reflected here?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never drew my conclusions from assumptions, and I think that this way of drawing conclusions is unacceptable. As for linking registered injuries with the cause of death, I commented on that earlier during my testimony but I may repeat. This formulation which is generally accepted among us and which I use is saponification, skeletonization, or putrefaction and you conclude on the basis of that, that the cause of death cannot be ascertained, but one may say that a gun-shot injury was found in the area of the head so there is some basis to conclude that the injury in the form of an entry or exit wound may have caused death.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me now understand you clearly. If you find a gun-shot injury in the head, you say there's some basis to conclude that injury may have caused death. Would you take such a conclusion -- let's just assume that we have a body without any other injuries, just that, would you then find it professionally acceptable to say, This has caused death?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It may be assumed so, but not with any certainty. Because we've had situations in the war area that, because of anger or some other reason, people shot at dead bodies. That's why conclusions are drawn in this way. And it's up to the person in charge of investigation to conclude on the basis of witness testimonies and so on, that death was caused by the entry and exit wound to the head. So, in those terms, such a conclusion is all right, and we have nothing against it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, how frequent would that be, that people started shooting at bodies which were dead already but which did not show any signs of other injuries apart from then what you assume may have been post-mortem injuries? So that person should have had a heart attack or something of the kind. How -- how -- do you have any -- could you give us any idea about the frequency of that happening; and, if so, on what basis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have had an opportunity to receive such information from people who were present when such acts were perpetrated, and I heard that while performing autopsies. That happened four or five times. As for the other information, I couldn't tell you whether somebody who had had a heart attack wasn't hit by a bullet. I don't have such information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The frequency, so you heard of some cases.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have heard that people shot at dead bodies who had previously died. Perhaps also by gun-shot injuries, but for some reason, they then shot at the dead bodies. I would not go into details as to the reasons, whether it was rage or somebody's whim, or an attempt at additional revenge because they had lost their loved ones, I really couldn't go into that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you say these cases, they may have been killed before by other gun-shots. So in my example where you have only one gun-shot, that would not fit into your examples.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there is only one gun-shot injury and if it's evident that it is so and if the soft tissues structures are present, then it would be normal that the death was caused by a bullet shot from a hand-held fire-arm and the damage that that caused to centres in the brain that are of vital importance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And now I come back to my initial question about frequency. Can you tell us anything more than that you heard about it a couple of times?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you see, we performed autopsies of mortal remains under wartime conditions only once that the bodies had been collected. So when we performed the autopsies of the remains, the people who brought the bodies and those who were in charge of investigation would point out this detail to us and tell us whether certain persons shot at those bodies, which they verified. So that was the information I received from others, and I wasn't personally present when somebody shot at dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Although it's not a precise answer to my question about frequency but following up on your answer, how would those who brought in the bodies, how they know whether someone had been shooting at a dead body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In principle, we did not have special teams that carried the bodies of those who lost their lives in armed conflict. It was the other combatants who were present and who then transported the bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And they told you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For example, in the area of Zvornik; then in the Sarajevo area; and then also in Ugljevik area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And may I take it that you then reported that in your autopsy report? That this is what we found but we received information that the injury was inflicted after the person had died? Did you record that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think not. Because I described all the gun-shot injuries in the autopsy report. All the injuries that I could find on the body were described in the autopsy report. On the basis of those gun-shot injuries, I then determined whether they were inflicted in life, if there was such a possibility, or if they occurred in death. And those -- the one who is supposed to note and verify such details was the person who was in charge of the investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you didn't mention that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But for complete information of those reading the forensic reports, it would be important to know that in relation to this specific body, information was received that gun-shot injuries, at least according to that witness, would have inflicted, post-mortem.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the investigation organs who are in charge of the investigation have the obligation to include that type of information in their report. It is up to me to describe all gun-shot injuries that were registered and to describe them in detail, if possible. So absolutely all of them. It is my duty to draw up a report from which one could conclude what kind of injuries are present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I could follow up on Judge Orie's questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: He asked -- if I'm reading the transcript correctly: "But for complete information of those regarding the forensic reports it would be important to know that in relation to this specific body information was received that gun-shot injuries or at least according to the witness would have been inflicted post-mortem?" The question I have for you is as a forensic pathologist, in your review of that body or any body, do you indicate an opinion as to whether wounds are ante-mortem or post-mortem?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it's possible for me to determine whether some injuries were inflicted in life or in death, I would then include that finding in my final opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And how does a pathologist looking at injuries -- what factors, what ante-mortem factors would one look for to indicate that a wound was sustained during the course of one's life?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are so-called absolute and relative reactions that occur in life. The absolute reactions are described by Professor Dunjic on page 17. Those are vital functions that were still preserved, and they imply certain signs on the body. Contusions, inhalations, swallowing of items of food or earth, bleeding around injuries, inflammation. That's the basis on which one determines that the injury occurred in life, if there are any such signs present. If they are not present, then the injuries occurred post-mortem, that is to say, in death.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just get clarification on that. Those attributes that you are mentioning, Mr. Stankovic, seem to relate to a well preserved body. What would be the attributes in a skeletonized body that show that the injuries were either ante-mortem or post-mortem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If we are dealing with a skeletonized body, we cannot determine whether an injury occurred during life, but in that case, you would describe in detail all the injuries, the entry canal of the bullet, in case of gunshot injury, and based on that you verify in your finding which injuries were found on what parts of the body, or which kind of instrument or weapon was used; and that, in combination with witness statements, would help the investigation to connect the injuries to the circumstances of the case being investigated by a prosecutor's office or judicial body. So with a skeletonized body, we do not pronounce ourselves on whether the injury occurred during life but we describe all the injuries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, relative to that point, at page 29, starting from line 3 of today's transcript, Mr. Ivetic read to you a quotation from Professor Dunjic's report which says: "It is also important for the Tribunal to note the existence of the so-called post-mortem injuries. These are injuries inflicted on the body after the cessation of the main vital functions. They can have all the characteristics, especially in case of bones, of fractures that occur in living people but without ante-mortem attributes." There any ante-mortem attributes that can be found in a bone -- in -- injured bone that indicates whether the injury was inflicted post-mortem or ante-mortem? This is now a skeletonized bone. And I'm asking you this question because you said that you agree with this proposition by Dr. Dunjic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think what I said and what Dr. Dunjic said is one and the same thing. Attributes like colouring in the colour of blood of the surface of the bone which was injured could indicate - that is to say, the strong blood colour - could indicate that the injury occurred during life, but it's not an absolute indicator and it belongs with vital reactions during life, such as inhalation, inflammation, thrombosis, et cetera. It could be an indicator but cannot be accepted with certainty because the colouring in the colour of blood would also occur in a person who sustained a gun-shot injury during life and sustained the same injury immediately after death, there will, in both cases, be a colouring of that spot in the colour of blood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When you talk about immediately after death, it seems like you're talking about a well preserved body. My question really is focussed on a skeletonized body mainly because Professor Dunjic talks of fractures to the bone and doesn't refer to soft tissue. And the nap of my question is: Are there ante-mortem attributes that could be used to determine whether or not an injury was inflicted post-mortem or ante-mortem? Now, the attributes that you given so far as I indicated at the beginning relate to a well preserved body. I'm asking if there are such attributes with respect to a skeletonized body.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Such attributes do not exist in a completely skeletonized body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you said you agreed with this proposition by Dr. Dunjic, where he talks of ante-mortem attributes which would not be found if the injury is inflicted post-mortem.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These ante-mortem attributes could be only if we didn't have the colouring in the colour of blood at the place of fracture. I don't know what else the attributes would be. It's one of the basic attributes to look at when you examine a skeletonized body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you don't know what the attributes would be, what is it you are agreeing with when you answered Mr. Lukic [sic] by saying -- Mr. Ivetic by saying, no, I agree with these two paragraphs as written by Dr. and Professor Dunjic. That's what you say at line 10 of that same page, 29, that I referred to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I just take a look once again?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That would be on page 18 in Serbian, the third and the fourth paragraphs from the top.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "They can have all the characteristics, especially with fractures, as when the person was alive ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Keep on reading.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is that the part?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That is the part. But you've got to read the next phrase.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The in-life nature of fractures cannot be determined based on only on the lines on the skull and that's the main objection to the work of the pathologists who did localisation on Srebrenica. "The same or very similar injuries can be inflicted by shrapnel, a blunt instrument, et cetera. They can occur also just after death, perimortem when the lines of fracture have the same appearance. The colouring in the colour of blood of the soft tissue around the injury in very decomposed bodies must be interpreted very relatively and cannot be treated as in life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But that's not the paragraph. Sorry, let me interrupt you, professor. I think you're reading a different paragraph. The paragraph we're referring to the one above which says: "It is also important for the Tribunal to note the existence of the so-called post-mortem injuries. These are injuries inflicted on the body after the cessation of the main vital functions, they can have all the characteristics (especially in case of bones) of fractures that occur in living people but without the ante-mortem attributes." And your response to this phrase, this paragraph, when asked by Mr. Ivetic as to what your opinion was, you said you agreed with it. Hence my questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... now you say in skeletonized bodies, you are not aware of any attributes that can be found to determine whether the injury is ante- or post-mortem.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because we don't have the soft tissue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... my question relates to skeleton -- because he is talking about a fracture to the bone. He is not talking about soft tissue. He is saying the fracture on the bone has no ante-mortem attributes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: With all due respect to Your Honour, I don't think that's what being said I think when you introduced this, we read this paragraph and you said to go to the next one which the witness did. So I don't know whether the confusion lies but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there for a second, Mr. Ivetic. Indeed, that's what Judge Moloto said but I think he referred to leaving out the last six words. That is, "but without the ante-mortem attributes." And then the witness started reading the next paragraph, whereas, apparently Judge Moloto invited the witness to read the last few words of the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And this is where I think the confusion is coming in because we're been talking about ante-mortem attributes in soft tissue. And so I'm confused because I'm hearing the same thing. There has not been any change.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In this paragraph, which you, Mr. Ivetic, quoted to Mr. Stankovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- it refers strictly to bones, fractures to the bones, and you asked his position on that paragraph. He said he agreed with it. And each time he has now introduced soft tissue, I've tried to say to him, that's not the point of my question. My question is on a skeletonized body.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in relation to this paragraph, Your Honours, I do have to stress the part that you are stressing "... but without ante-mortem attributes," according to the testimony of the witness is the tissue. So we can't say he is talking about stuff not in relation to tissue when ante-mortem attributes are mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Stankovic, what was read and to what you agreed, would you agree that if you have a skeletonized body, that it may be extremely difficult to establish whether there are any ante-mortem attributes which, therefore, would make it difficult to finally establish whether those injuries were inflicted post-mortem or ante-mortem, if you only have a skeletonized body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've said that it's very difficult to make a distinction on a skeletonized body between ante-mortem and post-mortem injuries. I've been saying this all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And with all due respect, that's what these paragraphs say as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put a question now to the witness. At the beginning of your testimony, you told us that you have carried out thousands of autopsies. Did you ever come across a case where you found that a person died and later on were shot at the head?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it was with the bodies that I worked on in Brcko. The location was Grbavica village where we found 13 bodies. I think that's when I made the finding that first some other injuries occurred and then a projectile was fired into their head or some other part of the body. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You say "some other injuries occurred." Which kind of injuries are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think there was one body that was decapitated, and after that, gun-shot injuries were inflicted in the chest; maybe also in the head, I'm not sure. I remember the name. It was a man called Pudic, and Perica Jovicic, one of the two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: These are the cases you are referring to. Thank you very much. You have answered my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you one other question. If you shoot someone in the head and we assume that he may have -- that he dies from that, if you shoot at him again 20 seconds later, do you consider that -- do you call that post-mortem, or do you call that perimortem, or do you -- and are you able, on the basis of your forensic analysis, to make a distinction between which shot hit the person of which he may have died and the other shot, which was inflicted 20 seconds, 30 seconds, perhaps, later?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's almost impossible to distinguish between the first and the second shot for several reasons. I won't go into details now. Because, first of all, we don't know within those 20 seconds after the first shot, the person could still show signs of life. The second gun-shot injury to the head, I couldn't say whether it occurred after death. I would, rather, describe it, and if it's a fresh body, I would say that it's the immediate cause of death. The immediate cause of death would be the gun-shot injuries to the head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Both of them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, both of them. Gun-shot injuries to the head would be listed as the immediate cause of death. I would not be able to say whether it was the first or the second because the interval between them is very short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think it's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is, indeed, time for a break. First of all, Witness, we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I am aware that we've stolen some of your time -- well, we've used some of what is not your time --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Our time, everyone's time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, everyone's time. Could you give us an indication as to how much more time you would need?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think 45 minutes or so should suffice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then ... One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Most likely -- and, of course, unforeseen circumstances not included, we'll take a break now and resume at quarter to 12.00, and we'd like you to finish your examination-in-chief in the next session. Then -- assuming that we're not absorbing time, and then that cross-examination would start tomorrow. As I announced earlier, we might -- we started early also in order to be able to conclude but to adjourn a little bit earlier today, so that's what was on our mind at this moment. We take a break, and we resume at quarter to 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Professor, now I propose that we look at part 3 of the Dunjic report. So I'd like to turn to page 24 in both languages, and the part I want to deal with is entirely on page 24 in the Serbian and it will be the last three paragraphs in relation to NKS 2-012 in the English, and it will continue onto the next page and conclude while discussing NKS 2-013. In relation to these cases and what is written in Dr. Dunjic's report, what are your professional opinions and/or comments as to the same?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's about two autopsy reports that contain practically the identical description of injuries to the head and in one report, it's NKS 2-012, it is concluded that the cause of death is the injury to the head inflicted by a bullet from a high-velocity weapon, and in NKS 2-013, the same pathologist,Dr. Kirschner, states the cause of death as extreme trauma to the head. From the description of injuries it is not impossible to make such findings, that one is a gun-shot injury, and the other is extreme trauma to the head. Now, I can read out the contents of the autopsy report, but I believe this is the main objection to this way of drawing conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I could seek clarification. You are recorded in the English transcript as having said: "From the description" -- just lost it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think we've lost part of the -- part of the answer between lines 20 and 21.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps you put the question again and you will receive a proper answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think that's the best way to proceed. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you the question again and ask you to repeat your answer and that is: What are your professional comments as to these two cases given the description of the injuries and the conclusions reached.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first case, NKS 2-012, traumatology report reads: "External fracture of the skull with fragmentation. Bones of the middle part of the face are missing except one part of the upper jaw. The -- one part of the skull is preserved but the whole left part of the crown and part of the occipital bone are missing. Fracture of the lower" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could -- could the interpreters please ask for this text to be displayed somewhere because we don't have it on the screen and the professor is reading too fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Next page in English --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Next page in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you slowly start reading again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean the second case? Shall I read it again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "In the case NKS 2-013, the same pathologist, Dr. Kirschner gives the following description. A traumatic defect of the skull 11 by 10 cm involving the left temporal, par. and occipital regions, linear fractures, radiating from the defect through the left and right parietal bones to the right temporal bone. Cause of death: Extreme trauma, to the head." This way of drawing conclusions, where we have two identical descriptions of the head in two different cases, in one case, the conclusion is drawn that the cause of death is a gun-shot injury to the head, and in the second case, the cause of death is listed as extreme trauma to the head. I don't see from which finding these conclusions are drawn and why the conclusions on the injury differ in view of the same descriptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I think we have it clearly. Now, I'd like to turn to page 27 in the English and it will relate to the third bold-faced paragraph in the middle.
