And in Serbian, it's page 27 near the bottom and it relates to Dr. Dunjic's comments as to the testimony of Dr. Lawrence in the Karadzic case: "Also at the same trial, on 8 December 2011, in reply to a question from the accused Radovan Karadzic, he said that 'it is not possible to establish the exact interval between death and burial'." Do you agree that it is not possible to establish the exact interval between death and burial as in regards to this part of Dunjic's report.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's page 25 in Serbian?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: 27 near the bottom in Serbian. 27 in e-court which would, I think, be page 20 -- one moment. Let me just find the English and I'll find the Serbian real fast. It's beginning of 27 ... December ... that is on page 26 in the hard copy and it's going to be the third paragraph from the bottom: [Interpretation] "...also at the same trial on 8 December 2011..." [In English] Have we found that now, professor?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you agree with Dr. Lawrence that it is not possible to establish the exact interval between death and burial in the instance that is being discussed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I take the witness back to the previous incident. You said in relation to the -- the -- the previous case we discussed that the descriptions in the two cases are identical. Now, I see that they are referring to similar damage to the head but they're not identical, are they? The one gives sizes of the impact. They're not identical, are they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said almost identical. They're not identical but they are nearly identical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At the very bottom of the same page in English and it will be paragraph 3 on the 27th page in Serbian from the top. And that will be -- and that will be 27 in the hard copy. It will be 28 in e-court and it will be the third -- excuse me, the second full paragraph from the top which in Serbian starts: [Interpretation] "Item 14 of the same document." [In English] And then I'll continue reading in English. "Item 14 of the same document" - the ERN number is given - "by Dr. C. H. Lawrence reads as follows: Six remained with an undetermined cause of death. In my opinion, these six cases probably represent perforating gun-shot wounds in soft tissue which can no longer be recognised because of loss of soft tissue and absence of boney damage." Then the -- Dr. Dunjic indicates: "This kind of assumptions and opinions, for which no professional evidence or explanation has been provided, seemed contradictory. A perforating wound in soft tissue, but the soft tissue has been lost due to putrefaction, and there is even absence of boney damage? On what bases did he then form his opinion and establish that these are perforating wounds? " What would be your professional comments as to these findings by Dr. C. H. Lawrence and the documents by Dr. Dunjic.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the comments of Dr. Dunjic and based on the findings of Dr. Lawrence, it follows that the mortal remains that were examined did not have any soft tissue on them and after that Dr. Lawrence concludes that it was probably a perforating wound of the soft issue inflicted by a fire-arm that can no longer be recognised because of the loss of soft tissue and absence of boney damage. This type of conclusion is unacceptable because if there is no soft tissue based on what do you then conclude that these perforating wounds existed on the soft tissue? There is no soft tissue on the bodies which were examined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But as you correctly said, he says probably. He doesn't make a definitive conclusion. He says probably.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In forensic medicine, there can be certainty, probability, and possibility, so these are various degrees of gradation. I cannot accept that someone should make such findings without the soft tissues being available. Possible or possibly or probably, that's a very wide notion. Let me not explain in detail what that means, but I see no reason why Dr. Lawrence would state this. No soft tissue is present in the examined mortal remains. No damage to the bones. That means that one cannot talk about gun-shot injuries with any certainty. I don't see why it's a problem to say that or should one say: Probably but based on what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What you're telling us is that the forensic findings do not support that probability. That's ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- clear [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could look at part four of the Dunjic report found at page 29 in the English and page 28 in the Serbian, what comments do you have on the material in this part of Dunjic's report that is the part that says, "Inconsistency in the report of Prosecution investigator D. Janc."

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Dr. Janc is a policeman and he mentioned some activities that he was involved in as a police officer. This has to do with the bodies, whether they died in 1995 or some other year. I wouldn't state my opinion about that because that's not within the purview of what a forensic medical specialist normally does.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could look at page 31 at the bottom in English and page 30 in the Serb version, and it will be the fourth paragraph up from the bottom on page 30 in the Serb, and it will be in relation to Bljeceva. "Similarly, document number KTA 672/04 of the Tuzla cantonal prosecutor's office states that the Bljeceva 1 site contains remains that are not related to the fall of Srebrenica. A total of 39 bodies were found there. The document includes the information that the body designated as," then there's a designation "belongs to an individual who was tied with ligatures. It also states that several bodies," and then identifying numbers are given, "were in plastic body bags marked," if we can go to the next page in English, "ZOV. The document notes that the former ICTY Srebrenica investigation team leader Alistair Graham visited the site on 23 July 2004." Now, Professor Stankovic, at the beginning of your testimony, we talked about the origin of plastic body bags marked ZOV, and at transcript page 43278, you told us these -- those were used in 1992 and were used up later that year. What question does this raise in your mind, the presence of ZOV body bags in a grave linked to Srebrenica which apparently the Tuzla prosecutor's office is convinced are not related to the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only say what I have said before, namely, that the army had those bags, that it supplied the area of Eastern Bosnia with the bags and that in 1992 all the supplies had been exhausted, and there's nothing more I can say about the bags that were found in the Bljeceva grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If we can turn to page 34 in the English, the fourth paragraph from the bottom, and in Serbian it will be 33 and the fourth paragraph from the bottom as well, and we have here: "When bodies are putrefied, decomposed bodies and body parts, the cause of death cannot be established with certainty and the opinion must be given very provisionally as I have already written but all pathologists and even anthropologists, including archaeologist R. Wright, categorically speak of perimortem injuries - i.e., injuries occurring during life and immediately before death (died from gun-shot wounds [sic]) this is unacceptable from the professional standpoint." Professor, what are your comments as regards to this part of Dr. Dunjic's report?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have tried today to provide an answer, but obviously it was not comprehensible. I can just repeat one more time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For the Chamber, it was comprehensible, but Mr. Ivetic, again, asked the question, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I was left wondering, given the last session, if that was clear at all, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I think we dealt with the matter in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Then, I will move on and save us time. Thank you, Your Honours, for assisting there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will then move to part 5 of the Dunjic report and page 38 in the English and the third paragraph from the top. And it will be page 36 in the Serbian and the third paragraph from the top of the page in the Serbian. And here Dr. Dunjic is drawing attention to the fact that Dr. Clark stated that he did not know about the armed conflict between the two warring parties in the critical period between 11 and 17 July 1995. And goes on to say: "According to his assessment around 5 per cent were hit by shrapnel. On 20 February 2007, the same pathologist, J. Clark, said in court 'that there were not many people who been wounded before that' ... ' for the vast majority death cannot be linked to combat'." And then Dr. Dunjic has some comments about this. What would you like to say as to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I'm a bit confused. You refer to part 5 and page 38 in English. And for me --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Part 6, I apologise. Part 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Part 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It is page 38 in English and third paragraph from the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yeah. Thank you. I was confused about what part we were in.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: As was I, apparently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Professor, do you have any comments as to this section.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these were Dr. Clark's observations, whether he was aware or not of the existing war conflict between the two warring parties. I believe he was not aware, if that's what he says. And as for his position, that for the majority, it could not be ascertained whether death had anything to do with combat. It would be good if Dr. Clark had said what was the percentage of the people whose death could be linked to combat and who were the ones whose death could be linked to execution or something else. I believe that on the basis of all the material that he had at his disposal, he could have stated this with a certain degree of likelihood. He may have composed a table showing that, which would have been very useful.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At the same page at the bottom in English and the same page in the Serbian, the second paragraph from the bottom, it is recorded again in relation to Dr. Clark: "It was possible to show that at least the vast majority had died a violent death, mostly from gun-shot injuries, but with a substantial number from blast injuries caused by shells." Now, keeping that in mind, I'd like to turn to page 40 in English, the second paragraph from the top, and page 38 in the Serbian at the top, and I want to look at the middle of the statement that's Enver Adzic ERN number 0037746748 that is listed where he describes: "Sometime around 1000 hours on the same day, a Chetnik paramilitary unit opened strong artillery fire at the remaining brigades and civilians who were in Buljim at the time. 1.000 soldiers and civilians in his assessment. They were shelled from PAMs," which we are told are anti-aircraft machine-guns, "PATs," which we are told are anti-aircraft guns, "Pragas, Zoljas," which we are told are hand-held rocket-launchers, "and RPGs ... the source (witness) also pointed out to us that his group had five automatic rifles which they fired at the direction of the Chetniks and thus covered their retreat deep into the woods but Refik's body was left behind, lying on the spot where he was killed." The question I have for you, sir, is if you know: Can this weaponry that this witness -- that this individual talks about being used at Buljim account for the type of injuries that we just looked at where it was said that a substantial number were from blast injuries caused by shells?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. MacDonald.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I think my friend should add to the original quotation from Professor Dunjic's report that he read that Professor Clark was speaking only about three graves in particular at the time. Those three graves being Ravnice, Glogova and Zeleni Jadar. The way the question is currently phrased, it could be taken that the vast majority that we are discussing is the entire set of victims pulled out of all of the Srebrenica related graves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would agree with that, and I apologize for not putting it at the top. With that clarification, then, I think the witness can answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The injuries noted by Dr. Clark could have been caused by the weaponry listed by you, the PAMs, PATs, Pragas, Zoljas and RPGs.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now I'd like to turn to page 45 in the English, second paragraph from the top, and it's the bottom of page 41 in the Serbian dealing with Mr. Baraybar, and, in essence, the objection by Dr. Dunjic is: "It should be said here that this is very difficult, almost impossible, to establish on putrefied and skeletonized corpses, even for forensic pathologists while he is an anthropologist. Hence in my opinion, in his comments regarding this issue, he overstepped his expertise."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What page are we at in English?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In English, it will be page 41 ... pardon me, 45 in English, 45 in English. It should be the second paragraph from the top under the heading, Jose Pablo Baraybar, and it talks about: "In his reports for specific sites Jose Pablo Baraybar anthropologist comments and explains the ante-mortem nature of gunshot injuries, both ante-mortem and/or perimortem, based on the appearance of the bones and established fractures. It should be said here that this is very difficult, almost impossible, to establish on putrefied and skeletonized corpses, even for forensic pathologists, while he is an anthropologist. Hence, in my opinion, in his comments regarding this issue, he overstepped his expertise." Do you agree, professor.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with the position that Dr. Baraybar overstepped his speciality considering that he is an anthropologist.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to look at page 47 in the English, the middle of the page, and page 43 in the Serbian, and it will be the second paragraph from the bottom, under examples, and here in relation to Hz-04 B262, it is recorded that Dr. Lawrence states: "On body parts and in the body bag, there were injuries consistent with injuries inflicted with violence and with homicidal intent including gun-shot wounds ..." What is your expert comment as to what Dr. Lawrence has stated here?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firstly, I think that forensic medical specialists are not those who are to determine intent. I think the court should decide on that on the basis of all available information. I have not seen a single reasoned explanation as to how and in what way evidence of violence inflicted on the body was destroyed. What were the injuries and how they occurred. If we consider that the bodies were exhumed and had been buried in mass graves. Is it possible that, during the burial and exhumation, injuries may occur on the body parts that had already been injured? That's usual and it is to be expected. Because if you have a gun-shot injuries to the head, it's realistic to expect that during burial in pits there might be light fractures of the bones because the integrity of the bone is already damaged, and even light pressure of soil or other bodies may cause additional injuries or damage that might look like deliberate destruction. But in this specific case, I would say once again I think that forensic medical specialists should not judge intentions unless they have information or evidence suggesting that readily available.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now I'd like to look at page 48 at the top in English and page 44 -- actually, it will be the ... it will be the fourth paragraph from the top in English, and it will be page 44 in Serbian, and it will be the second paragraph from the bottom in the Serbian. And it reads: "The report on this site mentions cases where blindfolds were found. Because the blindfolds were similar, in fact nearly identical on both sites HZ 04 and 05 (length, width, pattern), he was shown a photograph at the Radovan Karadzic trial, showing that the 'Mujahedin' who were then active in the BH wore bandanas, which he left without comment. This begs the question: Were the blindfolds, in fact, bandanas that had slid down after the process of putrefaction and decomposition of soft tissue?" Can you comment on this from a forensic medical point of view.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depending on the description of the blindfolds on the bodies that were found, one could say whether it was possible for a bandana that was tied around the forehead to fall to the area around the eyes or not. If the bandanas were tied across the earlobes, not above them but over them and tied at the back of the head, and tied tightly, then it could be stated with certainty that the bandanas were tied by another person. If the bandanas were above the earlobes and, if, after putrefaction, they may have loosened and may have fallen over the eyes, then it could be assumed, and it could be possible that bandanas tied in this manner fell over the eyes because the cartilage of the earlobes decomposes much later than soft tissues. But to repeat, it's necessary to look at the descriptions provided in the relevant documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could I ask you, in addition to this, wouldn't that also depend on the position of the body? I mean, it's gravitation that moves something in a direction, and I take that you're talking about gravitation, how it could come down. But that also depends on the position of the head, horizontal, vertical. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I fully agree with you. I just did not want to be too expansive in my answer. I only wanted to mention two possibilities. But, yes, I do agree with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, did you mention cartilage in the ears or in the earlobes?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Earlobes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I'd like to look at D339, page 3, with you. That would be a photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can have page 3 of the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In this image caught from a film, first of all, looking at the insignia on the uniform of this individual, do you have an opinion as to what warring faction this person is a member of?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judging by the look of the uniform, he is a member of the Muslim armed formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And looking at the cloth he has tried around his forehead, could you describe for us hypothetically what would happen to the positioning of that cloth if this person became deceased as the body begins to decay and putrefy?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If a person with this type of bandana where the widest part is in the area of the forehead was in a grave in a vertical position, placed vertically in the grave, once putrefaction occurred and considering that the bandana is in this specific case above the left earlobe, it is possible that such a bandana could fall over the eyes, in view of the putrefaction that caused the thinning of soft tissue structures. So it's possible for it to fall over the eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: One more photograph, D340 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before we do -- Are you aware of any bodies that were buried vertically in graves?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, when bodies are thrown into a mass grave, if they are buried in an orderly fashion, then they are placed one next to the other at a certain depth and in the lying position, lying on their backs. But if bodies are thrown into a mass grave, then it might happen that it is in a half-erect or in one of the erect positions or bent backwards or frontwards. So these would be cases of bodies that are not properly buried. We've had such cases in Glodjanska Brda. That's above Zvornik. We found there a mass grave with soldiers who were buried inside the trenches, and some of them were in sitting positions inside the trench. They were buried just so. We found them with their faces turned in all directions. So the archaeologists were the ones who did this. If we had information that this person was in such a position, as I described, which would follow from the exhumation report, then the body would be so. We could talk about what I talk about. If the body was leaning with its back and the explanation that I have provided would then follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could now have D340.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Can I ask you a question to you, Mr. Ivetic. Is it the position of the Defence that the blindfolds that were found in the grave are - the word identical is used in this paragraph - are identical to the bandanas?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: To which bandanas, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, you are showing us a picture of a bandana and the paragraph refers to Mujahedin having worn bandanas. Those bandanas that were worn by the Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I showed this picture and asked a hypothetical. I'm about to go specifically to Srebrenica if you like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand your question. I just want to get the thinking of the Defence on this issue. Is it the position of the Defence that the blindfolds found in the [indiscernible] are identical to the bandanas that were worn by Mujahedin at the time when this incident took place? That's the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If you take out Mujahedin, I will agree with you. It is the Defence position that certain pieces of cloth found in the mass graves can not excluded to be bandanas worn around the heads of combatants, not just the Mujahedins, during the time period. And as I said we're about to go to precisely Srebrenica and the column of men who left Srebrenica and look at a video still from that video of something that I think will address your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I go back to my question, is it the position of the Defence that those bandanas are identical with the blindfolds that were found? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Again, when you say those bandanas --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, the bandanas that I have been talking about here.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And without having the bandanas in the photographs, I can't make a determination but it's not the Defence's job to prove anything, Your Honours, we only have to establish reasonable doubt. And we say, yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to prove anything. I just want to find your position and if you don't want to tell me what your position is, that's fine. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think I've rather eloquently stated my position, and I will restate it: It is the Defence's position that the pieces of cloth found in the mass graves as to Srebrenica cannot all be excluded as potentially being pieces of cloth worn and the heads of combatants that were killed in combat and that in the graves then would go over the eyes or go off the body because some of the pieces of cloth were found loose in the grave, not affixed around heads. And we're about to look at a photograph of some survivors from the Srebrenica column with bandanas on their heads. Is that eloquent and sufficient enough for you, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Not for me. Thank you. Doesn't answer my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, then I don't know what other details to give.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Go ahead. Do your job, what you're going to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we look at D340, and this is a still from the Prosecution's Srebrenica trial video of actual members of the column of Srebrenica men as they arrived in Tuzla, and if we can look at pages 2 and 3 side by side, what is your opinion as to this cloth that this man has, if fellow members of the column of men leaving Srebrenica had the same or similar cloth on their heads and became deceased and were buried, would it be possible for that cloth to fall over the eyes of the bodies as they decompose? Again, given all the criteria that you've indicated in the answers to our previous questions about the positioning of the body.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot rule out the possibility that such a piece of cloth would slide down over the eyes, but I cannot say that with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's fine. That's fine. Now, in Dr. Dunjic's report on page 49 in English, the second paragraph from the top and on page 45 in Serbian, the fifth from the top in the number of paragraphs, do you have any comment as to the conclusions and opinions of Dr. Dunjic as expressed here in relation to ... the fact that some victims were perhaps killed inside the grave and that Baraybar and Wright said this based on projectiles found in a grave under a body. Do you have anything to say in relation to this?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only say that Mr. Baraybar and Dr. Wright are not forensic pathologists, and it's not within their area of expertise, so they are not able to speak about such things in view of their role.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now I want to move to part 8 of the Dunjic report which starts on page 50 in English and page 47 in the Serbian. And near the bottom of the page, Dr. Dunjic talks of some of the findings from a meeting of anthropologists and pathologists in 1997 in San Antonio which reviewed the work of the Prosecution experts. I would therefore like to look together with you and everyone at 65 ter number 20008, and I have a hard copy in Serbian, if it will assist us to move more efficiently. And the first question, professor: Are you familiar with this document, this report? Have you seen it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we have it first on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Oh. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's wait for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now that we have it on the screen, professor, have you seen this document before? Are you familiar with it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've had several occasions to read the report of the oversight committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we look at page 3 in the English and page 3 in the Serbian, we see a number of allegations listed, and I want to obtain your professional comment as to numbers 9 and 10 on the list. "Changing the written autopsy report by the supervising pathologist after the Prosecutor had departed," and "10, changing the cause and manner of death, again, after the prosecutor had been departed and had never been notified of those [sic] changes." What is your opinion as to these allegations and others in the report as they relate to pathologists?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. MacDonald.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, I heard my friend read out that it was after the prosecutor had departed, but I think the word is actually "prosector."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That is accurate. Prosector in both numbers 9 and 10. I apologise. I have a blurry copy in front of my and the screen is a little too far away for me to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Professor, what are your comments as to these and the other allegations contained in the report that relate to the work of the pathologists?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you ask a position on allegations. There are two questions. First, whether the allegations are true or not, that's one way of looking at it. And the other is that if they are true, what would it mean. I do not find that you have distinguished between that and asked for a general -- you put a rather general question. So could you please further refine your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes. I will be guided by Your Honours and rephrase my question to say --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If these allegations were true, as contained in the San Antonio report, how significant would you find that from a forensic medical standpoint?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm looking at what Dunjic said in his report. That's 47, page 47 in the Serbian version, and I will be commenting on that section. If Dr. Kirschner, with relation to the cause of death and manner of death, without precisely approval or consultation with the persons who actually did the autopsies as Gallagher stated, changed this then it would be a burden on this report. Nobody has the right to change somebody else's findings regardless of his capacity. If, like Milevski says, Dr. Kirschner exerted pressure on team members - or gave instructions, sorry - if he pressured team members who determined the cause of death, he had the right as team leader to express his opinion but the definitive position should be given by the person doing the autopsy. As for the tempo of exhumations being too fast that led to the co-mingling of the bodies, it's a professional problem that could have been solved. But that's something that could have been dealt with by the Prosecutor and he should have pointed out to Dr. Haglund that the speed of exhumations an autopsies was maybe too high.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. MacDonald.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: It appears the witness is reading. I'm not sure what he is reading from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think he --

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: He is also going outside the question by answering other allegations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What he has told us that he would look at Dr. Dunjic's report, what he said about it. Now, I think the question was focussing on numbers 9 and 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And the other allegations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the other allegations.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Apparently the witness is dealing with all of them. Perhaps no need to remind you, Mr. Ivetic, that we're already at well over seven hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's why I was trying to speed it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you try to take care that your focussed questions to the witness and, for example, to know that this witness thinks that if the speed is too much that someone else should have intervened might not be really within the expertise of that witness, although I can imagine that you find that. But let's try to focus on what is contentious.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay, professor, why don't we do it this way. Focussing on what Dr. Dunjic has specified in his report, that he has pulled from this San Antonio oversight committee report, or I should say, report of the oversight committee from San Antonio, if true, how significant would those issues be in your opinion from -- from a forensic medical standpoint?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in my view, it would be unacceptable, that kind of conduct. But whether they were acceptable in a specific job of work, it's probably up to the person leading that work to judge and to give an explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And ... in the -- the report we have in front of us, if we look at page 12 in both languages, and it's the committee recommendations under section 8, and we see a number of recommendations here. Now, this was in 1997, for future exhumations and excavations. The Tomasica investigation and autopsies occurred after these recommendations. In your opinion, based on what you saw in that review of that Tomasica evidence, how well were these recommendations adhered to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. MacDonald.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I object to that question as it's -- I think slightly misleading. These committee recommendations are with regard to mass graves exhumed under the UN and the war crimes tribunal as it was in 1995 and 1996 and so on. The Tomasica grave in 2013 was under the control of the national authorities, though Dr. Clark was there as well. So I'm not sure my friend isn't trying to compare two very different things here in this question, in asking the witness to comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, could you split up, and apart from the ambiguity in the question that how well were these recommendations adhered to could mean how well did they act in accordance, which was later recommended, or whether, as a follow-up of the recommendations they acted in accordance with them. And apart from the matter raised by Mr. MacDonald, perhaps you rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let me rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Taking into account what we discussed, I believe, yesterday, the testimony of Dr. Clark that he was involved in the investigations with the encouragement of the ICTY Prosecutor's office and ICMP, to what degree were the investigations in Tomasica undertaken with any of these recommendations in mind? Did you see any evidence of these recommendations being applied in that investigation?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think these recommendations are very correct. With regard to Tomasica, some of the points were accepted, the majority were not. And that led to the objections that I stated, speaking of Tomasica.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have already had this same document in evidence as D329 but without a Serbian translation. This version, which is a Prosecution 65 ter number, has the Serbian so I would ask that either this replace the prior exhibit or that the Serbian translation be attached to the prior, whichever formation works. But I think it would help us to have both languages in the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, what is the most suitable of dealing with it? Either to loosen it from this one and attach it to what is already in evidence, or to replace the English version which is in evidence by the new version which is both in English and in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would recommend the latter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then could you please -- you're hereby instructed to replace and could you help me with the number, Mr. Ivetic. D329.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To be replaced with what was on our screens which was?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're instructed to act in accordance with what I just said. Mr. Ivetic, we are well beyond the hour. We are well beyond the seven hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I have exactly four questions remaining.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's try to do that in the next five to six minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that we can conclude after five-quarters of a hour. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we return to the Dunjic report, D1448 MFI, and part 9 of the same, and that is at page 52 in the English and page 48 in the Serbian, and this is, again, item -- part 9 of the Dunjic report. What do you have to say about part 9 of Dr. Dunjic's reports? What would be your comments?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not say anything on this part, the number of victims killed between the 11 and the 19th July, because it's not within the area of expertise of a forensic pathologist.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we look at part 10 of the report, page 53 in Serb and page 57 in English, and I would ask you the same question in relation to this.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the same reasons. I believe that a different kind of expertise is necessary. Different experts should speak as to who died when, which information is in the possession of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and which information is in the possession of other institutions. That's not within the area of forensic pathology.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now I have a question as to page 68 onwards in English and page 63 onwards in Serbian, the opinions listed by Dr. Dunjic. What would you have to say about the opinion section of the report?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that we have already discussed enough. You know that I accept part of what Dr. Dunjic says, and there is a part that I didn't want to comment on because I believe it's not within the area of expertise because -- of a forensic pathologist, but Dr. Dunjic probably wanted to point out these issues that should somehow be cleared up by other experts. I wouldn't like to go into much detail because I believe that we have already discussed it. We would just be repeating ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I had forgotten to look at page 65 in English and page 61 in the Serbian and the questions posed by Dr. Dunjic, and these go on to the next page. Do you have a comment as to these?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think again that in my testimony I've already touched upon some of these questions and tried to answer some questions put to me by the Trial Chamber and the OTP, and I wouldn't like to deal with these questions. Because they follow from all the forensic expertise in the 11 sections that Dr. Dunjic's report consists of.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And with that, Your Honour, we would just put on the record that we will be tendering D1448 marked for identification, subject, of course, to the cross-examination and the procedure for Your Honours' decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Professor, I thank you. It's been a long three days, but I have no further questions in direct examination for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic, D1448 is already marked for identification. We will postpone our decision on admission until the end of the -- the conclusion of the evidence of this witness. Professor Stankovic, we'd like to see you back tomorrow. I give you the same instructions as before. But tomorrow it is 9:30 again and not 9.00. The instruction is that you would not speak with anyone about your testimony and I would understand that in a rather broad sense. I would not speak with outsiders on forensic pathology at this moment and wait until later. We'd like to see you back tomorrow, and we'll adjourn a bit earlier than usual. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Ivetic, this is one matter remaining. Page 61, line 21 of the transcript, says that: "I would have said I want to find your position, and if you don't want to tell me your position, that's fine. Thank you so much." That is what Judge Moloto said. I do agree with Judge Moloto. You didn't answer his question whether it's -- the bandanas were identical; but at the same time, a little bit later you gave an explanation, not on whether that was your position or not but on something else which at least assisted me to some extent, but that's then clear as well. We adjourn for the day, and we'll resume, tomorrow, Thursday, the 21st April, 2016, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
